paragraphs: This paper examines whether common crystal structure prediction benchmarks measure what researchers intend. The task is to generate likely crystal structures from a material’s chemical composition. Meaningful evaluation requires datasets that distinguish genuinely different structures and metrics that reflect structural diversity, rather than rewarding artifacts of how examples are stored or divided.

The authors identify three problems. Only about 40% of the widely used carbon-24 dataset consists of unique structures. In perov-5 and MP-20, many compositions have multiple structural forms, making random dataset splits inappropriate. They also show that a reported structure match rate can be misleading when identical building blocks exhibit structural variety.

The proposed fixes address both data and evaluation. Revised carbon-24 versions remove duplicates, vary how structures are represented, or split examples by atom count. Other proposed splits keep polymorphs together within each subset. Two new metrics, METRe and cRMSE, correct issues with match rate. Together, these changes aim to make benchmark results more informative about structure prediction ability.
neurips-2025-all-that-structure-matches-.tldr: Revised crystal datasets, more appropriate splits, and new metrics address misleading signals in structure prediction benchmarks.

paragraphs: The paper investigates why vision-language models can recognize image content well yet struggle with counting, spatial relationships, and selective attention. Drawing on cognitive science, the authors organize evaluation around perception, attention, and memory. Tests of leading models, including GPT-4o, reveal uneven abilities: some tasks approach ceiling performance, while others expose substantial gaps.

A central experiment separates visual interpretation from subsequent reasoning. Models that struggle to reason directly from an image improve markedly when they instead reason over captions they generated themselves. This result identifies a bottleneck in combining perception and reasoning, and supports developing stronger visual chain-of-thought abilities rather than treating visual understanding as a single capability.

Targeted fine-tuning on composite visual reasoning tasks moderately improves smaller models’ core cognitive abilities. However, these improvements do not produce large gains on difficult out-of-distribution benchmarks. Performance on the authors’ datasets nevertheless strongly correlates with results on MMMU-Pro and VQAv2, suggesting that the targeted evaluations capture abilities relevant to broader benchmark performance.
neurips-2025-caption-this-reason-that-vl.tldr: Vision-language models often reason better from their own captions, revealing a bottleneck in simultaneous perception and reasoning.

paragraphs: This paper studies vulnerabilities in how language models handle instructions from different contexts. The authors identify Tool-Completion Attack, a class of attacks that exploits function-calling mechanisms to redirect model behavior. They introduce a dedicated benchmark and find that even leading models remain susceptible, with high attack success rates in their evaluations.

Their proposed defense, Context-Aware Hierarchical Learning, builds an instruction hierarchy using contextual relationships between instruction segments. The approach balances understanding what a segment means with constraints associated with its role. This matters because interpreting instruction content and determining how much authority it should carry are connected parts of handling adversarial inputs.

Experiments report substantially stronger robustness against both conventional attacks and Tool-Completion Attack while preserving performance on general tasks. The method also generalizes strongly in zero-shot evaluations. These findings support context-sensitive instruction handling as a way to improve resistance across tested threats. The contribution combines an attack category, an assessment framework, and a learning approach that addresses the exposed weakness.
neurips-2025-context-aware-hierarchical-.tldr: Context-Aware Hierarchical Learning improves resistance to instruction attacks, including a newly identified attack on function calling.

paragraphs: Vision state space models process image patches as sequences, so the order in which they visit patches affects how they represent an image. Existing approaches commonly use manually designed scanning patterns. The authors argue that these patterns can disrupt meaningful spatial relationships and lack the flexibility needed to capture complex image structures.

Dynamic Adaptive Scan makes the scanning process depend on the data. It adaptively assigns both scanning orders and regions, giving the model more freedom to organize visual information. The method retains linear computational complexity and the ability to model relationships across the whole image, combining adaptive organization with the computational properties sought from state space models.

The authors build a vision backbone called DAMamba around this scanning method. Across image classification, object detection, instance segmentation, and semantic segmentation, it significantly outperforms popular vision Mamba models. It also surpasses some recent leading convolutional networks and Vision Transformers. The results indicate that scan design is a consequential part of adapting sequence-oriented models to visual tasks.
neurips-2025-damamba-vision-state-space-.tldr: DAMamba learns adaptive image scanning patterns to improve visual modeling while retaining linear computational complexity.

paragraphs: Sensitive information recognition systems must detect protected data even when its formatting has been altered to evade detection. The authors argue that existing datasets do not adequately cover these transformations, making it difficult to assess robustness. DataSIR supplies a benchmark focused specifically on recognition under diverse changes to data format.

The dataset starts with 131,890 original samples spanning 26 sensitive data categories drawn from multiple international regulations. Based on an empirical analysis of real-world evasion tactics, the authors implement 21 transformation methods. Applying these methods expands the collection to 1,647,501 samples, providing a much broader set of adversarial formatting scenarios for evaluation.

The authors evaluate four traditional natural language processing models and four large language models. For the latter, structured prompts vary the amount of contextual guidance to examine how prior knowledge affects recognition accuracy. Results show that DataSIR distinguishes performance among recognition algorithms. Its contribution is a shared evaluation resource for comparing systems across sensitive categories and transformed formats.
neurips-2025-datasir-a-benchmark-dataset.tldr: DataSIR tests sensitive information recognition using more than 1.6 million examples covering adversarial format transformations.

paragraphs: DICEPTION adapts a pretrained text-to-image diffusion model into a system for multiple visual perception tasks. The goal is to obtain strong generalist performance with limited task-specific training data and computation. Its starting point is a model already trained on billions of images, whose existing visual knowledge can support the new tasks.

Experiments comparing architectures and input designs identify preservation of that pretrained knowledge as central to successful adaptation. The resulting model reaches performance comparable to leading specialists. In the reported comparison with SAM-vit-h, it achieves similar results using 600,000 pixel-annotated images versus one billion, or 0.06% as much annotation data. This comparison concerns task training data alongside substantial prior pretraining.

Adapting DICEPTION to new tasks can require as few as 50 images and fine-tuning approximately 1% of its parameters. The authors also find that carefully applied classifier-free guidance improves depth and surface-normal estimation, while pixel-aligned training helps preserve fine details. These results show several ways to reuse generative visual knowledge efficiently for perception.
neurips-2025-diception-a-generalist-diff.tldr: DICEPTION preserves pretrained diffusion knowledge to support multiple perception tasks with limited additional data and computation.

paragraphs: Multimodal language models spend substantial computation processing visual tokens. Removing some tokens can make inference more efficient, but the choice of what to keep matters. The authors find that pruning methods driven primarily by attention often retain tokens with similar meanings, leaving a narrow representation of the image when pruning becomes aggressive.

HoloV addresses this problem by distributing the pruning budget adaptively across different spatial crops. Its selection strategy aims to preserve whole-image context alongside task-relevant information. This changes the emphasis from collecting individually prominent features to retaining a useful spread of visual evidence, reducing the loss of representational diversity that the authors identify in attention-first methods.

The framework is designed as a plug-in and is evaluated across multiple tasks, model architectures, and pruning ratios. The authors report stronger performance than leading alternatives. In one example, LLaVA1.5 retains 95.8% of its original performance after 88.9% of visual tokens are removed. That result illustrates how preserving context can improve the trade-off between computation and task performance.
neurips-2025-don-t-just-chase-highlighte.tldr: HoloV improves visual token pruning by preserving context across image regions instead of concentrating on similar high-attention tokens.

paragraphs: This paper addresses how to compute the best available trade-offs between fairness and predictive performance. A Pareto front describes choices where improving one objective requires sacrificing the other. The authors develop a method for finding this front without training complex models specifically to learn fair representations, making the trade-off itself the direct computational target.

The method begins with a theoretical analysis of optimal fair representations. Structural properties from that analysis reduce the Pareto-front calculation to a compact discrete problem. The resulting approximating problems can then be solved efficiently using existing concave-convex programming methods. This connects properties of ideal representations to a practical procedure for exploring attainable trade-offs.

The approach also applies directly to fair classification and supports any concave performance measure. That scope matters because the reduction methods discussed in the abstract depend specifically on the structure of accuracy. Evaluations on several real-world benchmark datasets compare favorably with recent fair representation and classification methods, supporting the practical value of the theoretical reduction.
neurips-2025-efficient-fairness-performa.tldr: A structural reduction makes fairness–performance trade-offs computable through compact optimization problems without training complex fair representation models.

paragraphs: Federated learning must combine updates from clients whose data differ and whose participation varies. These two features make optimization difficult: popular FedAvg-style methods can struggle to converge exactly and may need decreasing learning rates that slow progress. This paper studies how to model those dynamics and design an algorithm that handles them more effectively.

The authors represent participation and local updates using stochastic matrices and graphs that change over time. This mathematical description captures how information moves through the learning process. It supports a quantitative analysis of FedAvg’s limitations and provides the foundation for FOCUS, an algorithm built around a push-pull strategy for federated optimization.

The central result is a proof that FOCUS achieves exact convergence at a linear rate despite arbitrary client participation in the analyzed setting. Exact convergence concerns reaching the optimization target, while a linear rate describes geometric reduction of error. The contribution establishes that variable participation and heterogeneous data can be addressed together without accepting the convergence shortcomings identified for FedAvg-style methods.
neurips-2025-exact-and-linear-convergenc.tldr: FOCUS uses a graph-based push-pull formulation to establish exact, linear convergence under arbitrary client participation.

paragraphs: Industrial anomaly segmentation needs examples with pixel-level labels, but real defects can be scarce, varied, and expensive to annotate. Synthesizing anomalies offers another source of training data. The authors identify two obstacles: balancing generation quality with sampling speed, and treating anomalous regions and background uniformly despite their different statistical properties.

FAST combines two modules to address these obstacles. Anomaly-Informed Accelerated Sampling is a training-free sampling procedure that uses coarse-to-fine aggregation to accelerate diffusion’s reverse process. It can generate high-quality anomalies for segmentation in as few as ten steps. The Foreground-Aware Reconstruction Module adjusts anomaly-related noise inside masked foreground regions at every sampling step.

The foreground adjustment preserves localized anomaly information as denoising proceeds, supporting control over where and how a defect appears. Evaluations across multiple industrial benchmarks find that FAST consistently improves downstream segmentation over existing anomaly synthesis methods. The reported benefit therefore concerns the usefulness of generated examples for learning segmentation, alongside the reduction in sampling steps needed to produce them.
neurips-2025-fast-foregroundaware-diffus.tldr: FAST combines accelerated diffusion sampling with foreground-specific noise control to generate anomalies that improve industrial segmentation.

paragraphs: A constrained optimization solution must satisfy its rules as well as achieve a good objective value. Traditional solvers can be too expensive for real-time use, while faster learned approximations may violate constraints. FSNet tackles this tension by making a feasibility-seeking operation part of the neural network’s solution procedure.

That operation solves an unconstrained optimization problem whose objective measures constraint violations. In effect, the procedure explicitly seeks to remove violations while remaining differentiable, allowing it to participate in end-to-end training. The authors provide feasibility and convergence guarantees for the approach. This connects the speed-oriented learned solution process with an explicit mechanism for enforcing the original problem’s constraints.

Experiments cover smooth and nonsmooth problems as well as convex and nonconvex ones. FSNet produces feasible solutions with quality comparable to traditional solvers, and sometimes better quality, at substantially faster speeds. These results suggest that embedding feasibility into the solution process can make learned optimization more practically useful when a fast answer must also obey the problem’s requirements.
neurips-2025-fsnet-feasibility-seeking-n.tldr: FSNet embeds a differentiable feasibility-seeking step into learned optimization to produce fast solutions with constraint-satisfaction guarantees.

paragraphs: Models of individual neurons’ activity aim to capture stable computational properties that relate to molecular identity and anatomical location. However, recordings also reflect differences among animals, experimental designs, and recording platforms. Models can overfit to these batch effects, making their learned representations less useful when applied in a different experimental setting.

The authors introduce an evaluation protocol that explicitly tests generalization to unseen animals and stimulus types. They also propose adversarial training: a discriminator seeks batch-related information in the representation, while the representation model learns to suppress that information. This training pressure encourages the model to retain intrinsic neuronal properties instead of experimental signatures.

The strategy is model-agnostic and compatible with major single-neuron representation approaches. The authors report significant improvements in robustness, addressing both how generalization is measured and how it is learned. More transferable representations could support prediction of neuron identity and location in living animals. The work also identifies potential for unified activity-based neuron atlases, without presenting that possibility as an already completed outcome.
neurips-2025-generalized-and-invariant-s.tldr: Adversarial removal of experimental batch information improves how single-neuron activity representations generalize across animals and stimuli.

paragraphs: Optimization methods can all eliminate training classification errors yet select different solutions. This paper characterizes that implicit preference for normalized steepest descent and its momentum variant in multiclass linear classification with cross-entropy loss on separable data. The focus is on how the optimizer’s choice of matrix norm determines the solution it approaches.

The authors prove convergence to classifiers that maximize margin relative to the corresponding p-norm, and establish convergence rates. Spectral Descent and Muon emerge as special cases that approach spectral-norm max-margin solutions. Thus, the analysis connects these algorithms’ update geometry to a precise preference among classifiers that successfully separate the training examples.

A key technical step reduces analysis of entry-wise and Schatten p-norms to analysis involving the max-norm, using relationships among these norms and the dual sum-norm. Extending the max-norm case to preconditioning yields a corresponding result for Adam. These are results for the stated multiclass linear setting, which the authors argue exposes matrix-optimizer behavior more transparently than binary classification.
neurips-2025-implicit-bias-of-spectral-d.tldr: On separable multiclass linear problems, Spectral Descent and Muon converge toward spectral-norm max-margin classifiers.

paragraphs: KnowMol addresses two weaknesses in molecular language model pretraining: textual descriptions that do not explain molecules adequately, and molecular representations that do not convey chemical information effectively enough. These weaknesses concern both sides of connecting a molecule to language. The paper develops a dataset and a representation approach to strengthen that connection.

KnowMol-100K contains 100,000 fine-grained molecular annotations covering multiple levels of chemical knowledge. The annotations provide richer links between molecules and their textual descriptions. Alongside this dataset, the authors introduce a chemically informative molecular representation designed to address shortcomings in existing representation strategies. The two contributions supply complementary forms of information for building the model.

The resulting multimodal model, KnowMol, combines these developments. The authors report superior performance across molecular understanding and generation tasks in extensive experiments. The findings support the value of improving both chemical descriptions and molecular encoding during model development. The contribution therefore extends beyond a model alone: it includes a resource for molecular annotation and a way to represent molecules for learning.
neurips-2025-knowmol-advancing-molecular.tldr: KnowMol combines 100,000 detailed molecular annotations with chemically informative representations to improve molecular understanding and generation.

paragraphs: A collaborative agent can score well on a task while behaving in ways its human partner does not prefer. This paper treats human preferences as a separate learning concern from environmental reward. It focuses on the difficult case where people provide only a small amount of recorded preference feedback and cannot participate in further online interaction.

The authors formulate a combined online-and-offline reinforcement learning problem while keeping the training regime entirely offline. Their framework alternates between learning from the recorded preferences and recovering the generalization associated with online learning. This alternation addresses the mismatch between limited human feedback and the agent’s broader learning objective, aiming to keep preference alignment and task generalization stable together.

The framework builds on existing reinforcement learning algorithms and is evaluated on a benchmark based on Overcooked, an environment for studying human-agent cooperation. The authors report strong performance across different preference styles and cooperative scenarios. The results support learning more preference-sensitive collaboration from limited offline feedback without requiring additional live interaction with human partners.
neurips-2025-learning-preferences-withou.tldr: Alternating preference learning and generalization recovery helps cooperative agents learn from limited human feedback without further human interaction.

paragraphs: Audio-visual speech recognition must balance the information retained in input tokens against the cost of processing them. Matryoshka representation learning lets one model operate at different compression levels, allowing that balance to change during inference. However, training each level independently limits knowledge sharing and can weaken performance when compression is high.

MoME adds a sparse mixture of experts to a frozen language model. A router selects a limited set of experts, alongside shared experts, to allocate capacity across modalities and compression levels. The shared router encourages consistent expert use across granularities, so heavily compressed inputs can benefit from representations learned when more information was retained.

Experiments on LRS2 and LRS3 report leading performance for combined audio-visual recognition, audio-only recognition, and visual-only recognition. The method also uses significantly fewer parameters and remains robust under noise. These findings support combining adjustable representations with selective expert computation: the model can vary input detail while sharing useful learning across scales, rather than treating each compression level as an isolated training problem.
neurips-2025-mome-mixture-of-matryoshka-.tldr: MoME shares expert knowledge across token compression levels to improve efficient, noise-robust audio-visual speech recognition.

paragraphs: Choosing a model configuration often involves balancing reliability against cost. Prior knowledge can suggest relationships among candidates: a longer prompt, for example, may provide more detail and therefore be more reliable. Existing selection methods do not always combine such structured information with formal statistical guarantees about the configurations they accept.

Reliability graph-based Pareto testing represents expected reliability and cost relationships as a directed acyclic graph. The graph is inferred from prior information and held-out data using a Bradley-Terry ranking model. These relationships guide exploration of the configuration space, allowing the selection procedure to use evidence about how candidates compare rather than considering their structure irrelevant.

The framework maintains reliability guarantees expressed through false discovery rate control. This is a statistical guarantee about erroneous discoveries in the selection process, rather than certainty that every accepted configuration is reliable. Experiments show significant improvements over learn-then-test and Pareto testing, attributed to more efficient exploration. The contribution combines structured comparisons, multiple objectives, and formal testing within one selection framework.
neurips-2025-multi-objective-hyperparame.tldr: RG-PT uses graphs of expected reliability–cost relationships to improve hyperparameter selection while controlling false discoveries.

paragraphs: PLEIADES is a class of neural networks designed for low-latency classification and detection from event-based data. Its temporal convolution kernels are generated from orthogonal polynomial basis functions. This gives the networks a structured way to represent how information across time contributes to an output, supporting online processing of spatial and temporal signals.

The structured kernels also provide flexibility in temporal resolution. The authors can change both the data sampling rate and the network’s discretization step without additional fine-tuning. This matters when the rate at which data is processed needs to vary: the model’s temporal construction supports that adjustment without requiring another round of adaptation.

Across three event-based benchmarks, the authors report leading results with substantially lower memory and computational costs. PLEIADES reaches 99.59% accuracy on DVS128 gestures with 192,000 parameters, rising to 100% with a small output filter. It reaches 99.58% on the AIS 2024 eye tracking challenge and 0.556 mAP on PROPHESEE automotive detection, demonstrating the approach across different temporal perception tasks.
neurips-2025-pleiades-building-temporal-.tldr: PLEIADES uses polynomial temporal kernels for efficient event-based perception that tolerates sampling-rate changes without fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Generalist robot policies can attempt many manipulation tasks, yet their success on unfamiliar tasks remains limited. A useful failure detector must recognize trouble early enough for a robot to stop, backtrack, or request help. The authors frame this as multitask failure detection, where a detector must transfer beyond the tasks and environments used for training.

Their analysis finds that vision-language-action models contain internal features carrying high-level information about success and failure across tasks. SAFE learns from these features using both successful and unsuccessful rollouts. It produces a single scalar representing failure likelihood, turning knowledge already present inside the policy into an explicit monitoring signal.

SAFE is evaluated on unseen tasks with OpenVLA, π₀, and π₀-FAST in simulation and real-world settings. The authors report leading failure detection performance against diverse baselines and the best tested balance between accuracy and detection time using conformal prediction. The results support internal policy features as a transferable basis for monitoring, with timely alerts enabling subsequent corrective actions.
neurips-2025-safe-multitask-failure-dete.tldr: SAFE reads robot policies’ internal features to detect likely failures on unseen tasks and balance accuracy with timely alerts.

paragraphs: Machine learning services often keep their models and clients’ data confidential. That confidentiality makes outside verification of fairness difficult. Existing confidential assessments can also rely on a fixed dataset, leaving them unable to guarantee fairness when deployment data change or a provider behaves improperly. Cryptographic verification can introduce a separate obstacle through computational expense.

The paper introduces online fairness certificates that assess fairness with respect to data actually received during deployment. This shifts the subject of certification from a static evaluation collection to the service’s ongoing inputs. The distinction matters because a certificate about earlier data need not establish the same property for the data a service encounters later.

OATH implements confidential online group fairness certification using a zero-knowledge proof protocol. It exploits statistical properties of group fairness through a cut-and-choose-style construction to improve scalability over baselines. The authors present the protocol as efficient enough for deployment. Its contribution joins operationally relevant fairness verification with confidentiality, addressing both the relevance of the certified data and the cost of certification.
neurips-2025-secure-and-confidential-cer.tldr: OATH provides scalable, confidential group fairness certificates for data received during actual model deployment.

paragraphs: Predicting language model performance from size and training data becomes difficult when model families use different training recipes. A single scaling law may miss these differences, while fitting a separate law for every family can require training several model sizes. Sloth seeks to reduce that burden by using publicly available benchmark results.

The method assumes that benchmark performance reflects a small set of underlying skills, such as reasoning and instruction following. Model size and training tokens influence these skills, but different families develop them with different efficiencies. Correlations among benchmarks help connect observed scores to shared skills, giving predictions a more interpretable structure than treating every benchmark independently.

The authors provide theoretical results on identifying the model’s parameters and evaluate predictions on 12 benchmarks from Open LLM Leaderboard v1 and v2. They report accurate predictions and insights into downstream-task scaling, additional inference-time computation, and compute-efficient skill development. The central contribution is a shared skill-based account of performance that still accommodates differences among model families.
neurips-2025-sloth-scaling-laws-for-llm-.tldr: Sloth predicts performance across language model families by modeling shared latent skills with family-specific scaling efficiencies.

paragraphs: SPTI generates differentially private synthetic images by moving the privacy-sensitive synthesis stage into text. The motivation is that existing private image generation methods struggle to produce high-resolution outputs that preserve the structure of the source data. Text descriptions offer an intermediate representation through which established private text generation methods can be applied.

The pipeline first captions each private image with an image-to-text model. A modified Private Evolution algorithm then generates differentially private text, and a text-to-image model converts that text into synthetic images. The method requires only inference with existing models, without model training, making it resource-efficient and compatible with proprietary models.

The reported quality improvements are substantial at ε = 1.0. On LSUN Bedroom, SPTI achieves FID 26.71 compared with 40.36 for Private Evolution. On MM-CelebA-HQ, it achieves 33.27 compared with 57.01 for private fine-tuning baselines. These findings support the textual intermediary as a practical route to higher-quality private image synthesis without training a new image generator.
neurips-2025-synthesize-privacy-preservi.tldr: SPTI turns private images into differentially private text and then synthetic images, improving image quality without model training.

paragraphs: T2I-R1 explores how reasoning and reinforcement learning can improve text-to-image generation. It divides the generation process into two reasoning levels: planning the prompt’s meaning at a high level and handling visual detail during patch-by-patch generation. This division connects decisions about what the image should depict with the lower-level process that produces it.

The model uses semantic-level chain-of-thought for planning and token-level chain-of-thought for pixel processing. To coordinate them, the authors introduce BiCoT-GRPO, which optimizes both reasoning outputs in the same training step using an ensemble of generation rewards. The training design therefore gives the two levels a shared optimization process rather than leaving their coordination implicit.

Applied to Janus-Pro, the approach produces reported improvements of 13% on T2I-CompBench and 19% on WISE, and surpasses FLUX.1 in the reported evaluations. These findings support the usefulness of jointly training high-level planning and low-level generation reasoning. The contribution is both a reasoning-enhanced generator and a reinforcement learning procedure for coordinating its two reasoning stages.
neurips-2025-t2i-r1-reinforcing-image-ge.tldr: T2I-R1 jointly reinforces semantic planning and token-level visual reasoning to improve text-to-image generation.

paragraphs: Tracking becomes difficult when several objects look alike, because appearance alone provides little basis for keeping their identities separate. This paper investigates motion information already learned by pretrained video diffusion models. The authors find that these models contain representations useful for tracking without task-specific training, offering a way to distinguish objects when visual appearance is ambiguous.

The key observation concerns the timing of information within denoising. Early stages, when noise is high, isolate motion, while later stages refine appearance. The proposed self-supervised tracker uses the motion representations exposed by this process. This makes the internal behavior of a video generator useful for a different task: following individual objects through time.

The tracker improves by up to six points over recent self-supervised approaches on established benchmarks and new tests focused on similar-looking objects. Visualizations also show tracking of identical objects through difficult viewpoint changes and deformations. Together, the results identify early diffusion representations as a useful source of motion cues for a challenging failure case in self-supervised tracking.
neurips-2025-video-diffusion-models-exce.tldr: Motion representations from early video diffusion denoising improve self-supervised tracking of similar-looking objects without task-specific training.

paragraphs: VLMLight addresses traffic signal control when routine efficiency must coexist with responses to safety-critical situations. Its image-based simulator provides multiple views of intersections, giving policies access to cues such as vehicle type, movement, and spatial density. These visual inputs support decisions that account for more than a simple summary of traffic volume.

A language model acts as a meta-controller, choosing between two decision branches. A fast reinforcement learning policy handles ordinary traffic, while a structured reasoning branch handles critical cases. In that branch, several language model agents work together to assess signal phases, prioritize emergency vehicles, and check compliance with traffic rules.

Experiments show emergency-vehicle waiting times reduced by up to 65% compared with reinforcement-learning-only systems. Under standard conditions, the framework preserves real-time performance with less than 1% degradation. These results support selective use of more elaborate reasoning: the controller can devote it to critical situations while retaining the responsiveness of the faster policy for routine traffic.
neurips-2025-vlmlight-safety-critical-tr.tldr: VLMLight switches between fast traffic control and collaborative language-model reasoning to improve emergency response while preserving routine performance.
